impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board's Penumbra framework—holding that Dynamic Drinkware's written description analysis does not apply to prior art determinations under AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(d)(2)—was correct, and what standard governs when a reference patent may rely on its provisional application's filing date for prior art purposes under the AIA.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination and remanded, addressing a critical question about when a reference patent can claim the benefit of its provisional application's filing date as prior art under the AIA. The decision creates uncertainty around the Board's Penumbra rule, which had lowered the bar for establishing earlier prior art dates. This is significant for IPR proceedings and patent validity challenges involving provisional application priority dates.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners may benefit from a stricter standard for opponents seeking to establish earlier prior art dates through provisional applications, potentially preserving more patents from IPR challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies challenging patent validity through IPR proceedings may face greater difficulty using reference patents with provisional filing dates as prior art, potentially increasing litigation costs and reducing the effectiveness of IPR as a defense tool.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 applies differently to method claims versus composition claims, and whether broad method claims reciting functional antibody limitations are adequately enabled when any member of the claimed genus would be effective for the recited treatment.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of its panel decision upholding Teva's broad method claims for treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies, over a dissent arguing the decision undermines enablement standards for method claims post-Amgen. The dissent warned the holding will sustain overly broad claims and undermine medical innovation. This decision has major implications for pharmaceutical and biotech patent scope.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies holding broad method-of-treatment patents benefit from a more permissive enablement standard for method claims, potentially preserving valuable patent portfolios covering broad therapeutic uses.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar manufacturers face broader blocking patents on therapeutic methods, potentially delaying market entry and increasing costs. Competitors may find it harder to challenge broad method claims for lack of enablement.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the licensed patents such that the licensee could sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether a shift to an enforcement-only business model constituted cessation of business operations triggering automatic termination of the license.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M conveyed all substantial rights, allowing it to sue without joining A&M. The court also held that shifting to a patent enforcement business model did not constitute ceasing business operations. This decision clarifies when exclusive licensees have standing to enforce patents independently and validates enforcement-focused business models.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent licensing entities and exclusive licensees benefit from clearer rules confirming their ability to enforce patents independently without joining the patent owner, and that pivoting to enforcement does not terminate a license agreement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a procedural defense based on standing challenges and license termination arguments, potentially increasing exposure to patent enforcement actions by licensing entities.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert testimony and in setting aside the jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving misappropriation of automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously excluded damages models. The court also reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury's award, while affirming the finding of trade secret misappropriation liability. This case is significant for trade secret valuation methodology and the interplay between trade secret and contract claims in software licensing disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and trade secret owners benefit from a broader range of acceptable damages methodologies, and the reinstatement of the jury's contract damages award reinforces the enforceability of software licensing agreements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop competing software after licensing relationships end face increased damages exposure, as courts may accept broader trade secret damages models on remand.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communications are eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and how the Alice framework applies to claims involving optimized signal processing techniques.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit issued a split decision on patent eligibility, vacating the summary judgment of eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents. The court also affirmed the jury's infringement and damages findings. This decision provides important guidance on the Alice eligibility framework as applied to communications technology patents and affects standards-related patent enforcement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to specific technical implementations in communications standards may benefit from the court's affirmance of eligibility for certain claim formats, providing a roadmap for drafting eligible claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing industry standards face continued uncertainty about patent eligibility for signal-processing innovations, and the vacated eligibility findings for some claims create risk for holders of similar patents.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Egyptian Goddess framework for design patent infringement improperly focuses courts on differences between designs rather than overall similarity, and whether functionality determinations in design patent claim construction present jury questions that cannot be resolved at summary judgment.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing in a design patent case, with a notable dissent from Chief Judge Moore arguing that Egyptian Goddess has shifted the design patent infringement inquiry toward differences rather than similarity, and that functionality determinations are factual questions for juries. The concurrence defended current precedent. This decision preserves the existing framework for design patent infringement analysis, which frequently resolves cases at summary judgment.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the preservation of the current framework, which allows design patent infringement cases to be resolved at summary judgment based on visual differences between designs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face a framework that the dissent argues systematically favors defendants by focusing on differences and resolving functionality issues without jury involvement, potentially undervaluing design patent rights.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims to a communications apparatus reciting transmission of signals 'over air' are invalid for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), even if they are not indefinite.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds raised by Samsung. The court held that while the claims were sufficiently definite, they were not enabled because the specification did not teach a person of ordinary skill how to practice the full scope of the claimed invention. This decision illustrates the Federal Circuit's willingness to affirm on alternative invalidity grounds and clarifies the interplay between indefiniteness and enablement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds, providing multiple pathways to invalidate overly broad patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face risk that claims surviving an indefiniteness challenge may still be invalidated for lack of enablement, requiring careful attention to specification disclosure breadth.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court properly awarded attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and sanctioned plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 for pursuing patent infringement claims involving a patent whose related applications had been rejected under § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal without leave to amend and the attorney fee award under § 285, and addressed the scope of sanctions against plaintiff's counsel. The court held that pursuing infringement claims with a patent whose related applications had been rejected on eligibility grounds, combined with inadequate pre-suit investigation, supported an exceptional case finding. This decision reinforces the consequences of pursuing weak patent infringement claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from enhanced deterrence against frivolous patent infringement suits, with the court endorsing fee-shifting and sanctions where patentees pursue claims despite clear eligibility concerns in related patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities and their counsel face heightened risk of fee awards and sanctions when asserting patents with related applications that have faced § 101 rejections, potentially chilling enforcement of patents in certain technology areas.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a dispute over the interpretation of a patent settlement agreement phrase 'survives the EPR' necessarily depends on resolving a substantial patent law question, giving the Federal Circuit subject-matter jurisdiction.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over a contract dispute regarding whether patent claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination, finding the dispute was fundamentally about contract interpretation under state law rather than patent law. The court transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. This decision is significant for structuring patent settlement agreements and understanding which court has jurisdiction over post-settlement disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies structuring patent settlements benefit from clarity that disputes over settlement terms will be resolved under state contract law rather than patent law, potentially leading to more predictable outcomes in regional circuits.
impacts.negativeImplications: Parties who assumed Federal Circuit jurisdiction over settlement disputes may face unexpected forum changes, and the decision introduces uncertainty about which courts will interpret patent-related settlement provisions.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulation imposing a 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in sunset reviews of antidumping duty orders conflicts with the governing statute.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade, holding that Commerce's 15-day filing deadline for sunset review participation was a valid exercise of agency authority because the statute is silent on timing. The decision reinstates Commerce's regulatory framework for sunset reviews of antidumping orders, which protects domestic industries from dumped imports. This has significant implications for companies in industries subject to antidumping orders.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers protected by antidumping orders benefit from clear procedural rules governing sunset reviews, and Commerce retains flexibility to administer the review process efficiently.
impacts.negativeImplications: Domestic interested parties face a strict 15-day deadline to participate in sunset reviews, and failure to meet this deadline could result in revocation of protective antidumping orders, exposing domestic industries to resumed dumping.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court provided sufficient reasoning in denying sanctions under Rule 11 and attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 where a patentee asserted a patent whose related applications had been rejected under § 101 post-Alice.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the denial of sanctions and fees, holding the district court's order lacked sufficient detail for meaningful appellate review. The court noted that Epic Tech had pursued infringement claims despite related applications being rejected under § 101, and the PTO had rejected claims of related applications on eligibility grounds before suit was filed. This decision signals heightened scrutiny of patent infringement claims where related patents face eligibility issues.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent cases benefit from increased accountability for patentees who pursue claims despite clear warning signs of invalidity, as courts must now provide detailed reasoning when denying fee and sanction requests.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face greater exposure to sanctions and fee awards, as the Federal Circuit requires district courts to carefully analyze whether pursuing claims with related § 101 rejections constitutes exceptional conduct.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly construed the claim term 'internal diameter' in a patent directed to oil and gas wellbore tools, and whether errors in claim construction affected the jury's infringement and validity findings.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's judgment of infringement and remanded for further proceedings, finding that the claim construction of 'internal diameter' required reconsideration. This case involves patents critical to the oil and gas industry's casing installation technology and has significant commercial implications for competing wellbore tool manufacturers.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in the oil and gas sector benefit from the Federal Circuit's willingness to scrutinize claim construction in cases with significant commercial stakes, potentially narrowing the scope of asserted patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the energy sector face uncertainty when claim terms have multiple plausible constructions, as the Federal Circuit may vacate favorable judgments and require further proceedings on claim scope.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may reach the merits of a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss for patent ineligibility under § 101 after already concluding that venue is improper and dismissing under Rule 12(b)(3).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's decision to dismiss on both improper venue and patent ineligibility grounds, holding that a court may address merits-based dismissal even after finding venue improper. The '979 patent, directed to e-commerce bridge computer methods, was found ineligible under § 101. This decision gives defendants a potential preclusive merits ruling even in improper venue dismissals.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from the ability to obtain merits-based dismissals on patent eligibility even when venue is improper, potentially precluding re-filing of weak patent claims in other jurisdictions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk of a merits-based eligibility ruling that could have preclusive effects, even when seeking to refile in a proper venue after a venue-based dismissal.
